# Methods

## Conceptual framework

Land ownership may affect farm performance through two distinct margins that an aggregate comparison cannot distinguish. The first is technical efficiency (TE), which captures how effectively farmers use the technology available to them. The second is the technology gap ratio (TGR), which captures how close the technology available to a farmer is to the best technology attained by any farmer in the sample [@Coulibaly2022; @Abdulai2010]. The potential effect of ownership on TE arises primarily through farmers’ control over land. Farmers who expect to cultivate the same plots over longer periods may have stronger incentives to maintain soil fertility, time farm operations appropriately, and supervise labour than those operating under temporary or contested tenure. Farmers without ownership, however, may respond to insecure or short-term tenure by intensifying inputs that are under their direct control, potentially narrowing the efficiency advantage that ownership would otherwise provide [@Selejio2022; @Kousar2018; @Ky2025].

Beyond these effects on how efficiently existing technology is used, ownership may influence the technology farmers are able to access. Secure ownership can facilitate investment by extending the horizon over which farmers can recover the returns to land-improving investments and by improving access to credit. These channels can encourage the adoption of improved seeds, machinery, and other productivity-enhancing technologies [@Feder1987; @Akber2024]. In contrast, insecure tenure can discourage investment because farmers face greater uncertainty over whether they will retain the benefits of future returns, while the absence of acceptable collateral may further restrict access to credit [@Isnaini2025; @Mhlanga2025]. Ownership may also improve access to extension services, market information, and other inputs that expand the technology available to farmers, independently of credit constraints [@Addae2026; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2022]. These mechanisms imply that ownership may affect both the efficiency with which farmers use existing technology and the technology frontier they can access. We therefore hypothesise that (H1) land ownership is associated with higher meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE), and (H2) that this advantage operates primarily through the technology margin, reflected in a higher TGR rather than a higher TE.

The extent to which these mechanisms operate, however, depends on what ownership means in practice. Ownership is not a uniform institutional condition, and the measures used to capture it may reflect different dimensions of farmers’ actual tenure security. Documentation is one such dimension. Where security derives from customary authority and social relationships rather than formal documentation, an undocumented farmer may enjoy protection comparable to that of a documented owner and therefore face similar incentives to invest [@Goldstein2008]. The rights attached to ownership provide another distinction. The ability to pledge or transfer land gives ownership financial and economic value, whereas an owner without these rights may have limited access to the credit and investment channels through which ownership is expected to affect technology. The mode of acquisition is also relevant, since purchased, rented, inherited, and family-allocated land may provide different degrees of security and different investment incentives even among farmers with similar documentation status [@Lawry2014; @Rondhi2018; @Lawin2018]. Finally, the extent to which ownership translates into productivity gains may vary with farmer and production characteristics, including gender, age, education, crop characteristics, and the functioning of local land and credit markets [@Deininger2023; @Nara2021; @Peters2022; @Nouf2023]. These considerations motivate our examination of ownership not only as an aggregate status, but also through its documentation, associated rights, and mode of acquisition.

## Meta-stochastic frontier analysis

A raw comparison between landowners and non-landowners conflates two things that are conceptually separate: how good the technology available to each group is, and how efficiently each group uses whatever technology it has. The meta-stochastic frontier (MSF) framework exists to pull these apart, comparing farm performance both within a tenure group and across groups that may not share the same production technology at all. The approach has an established applied record in agriculture, including Ghanaian maize [@TweneboahKodua2022], Ethiopian cereals [@Birhanu2022], and Bangladeshi dairy systems [@Uddin2014], each using group-specific frontiers and metatechnology ratios to make the same separation. `r xref("msf_results")` reports the full set of frontier estimates obtained here.

The construction follows the two-step MSF approach [@Huang2014] and proceeds in three stages. A stochastic frontier is fitted separately within the landowner group and within the non-landowner group, and each farmer's technical efficiency (TE) is read off against their own group's frontier, a measure of how well they convert inputs into output relative to others farming under the same tenure status. The two frontiers are then pooled into a single meta-frontier: the best production technology attained by any farmer in the sample, regardless of tenure. Each group's shortfall below that shared benchmark is its technology gap ratio (TGR) [@Battese2004]. Multiplying a farmer's TE by their group's TGR yields meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE), performance judged against the best technology in the whole sample rather than only against the farmer's own group. Because TE and TGR are estimated as separate quantities before being multiplied together, an MTE gap between landowners and non-landowners can be traced to whichever of the two, unequal technology or unequal efficiency, is actually responsible, rather than left as one undifferentiated number.

Within a tenure group we treat the production technology as shared across all farmers in that group, so that variation in management, not variation in technology, is what spreads farmers across different points along the group's frontier. Some farmers land below the frontier because of inefficiency or a one-off setback; others can appear to sit above it, not because their technology is better but because a favourable shock happened to raise their output that period. Prior studies of Ghanaian agricultural production using GLSS data have fitted both Cobb-Douglas and Translog specifications [@Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021b; @Ansah2023]; a likelihood ratio test here rejects Cobb-Douglas at the 1 percent level, so we proceed with the Translog. Left uncorrected, the Translog estimates violate monotonicity and quasi-concavity, so we impose monotonicity directly and check quasi-concavity after estimation using a standard three-step correction; once corrected, monotonicity holds for `r fmt_num(100 * min(unlist(objs$diagnostics$mono)), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100 * max(unlist(objs$diagnostics$mono)), 1)` percent of observations and curvature for `r fmt_num(100 * min(unlist(objs$diagnostics$curv)), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100 * max(unlist(objs$diagnostics$curv)), 0)` percent, depending on the frontier (`r xref("input_elasticities")`). The group-specific frontier for group $j$ is therefore a Translog:

$f^{j}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right) = \ln y_{\text{ijt}} = \beta_{0j} + \sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{\text{kj}}\ln x_{\text{kijt}}} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}^{}{\sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{\text{skj}}\ln x_{\text{kijt}}\ln x_{\text{sijt}}}} + \beta_{h}h_{\text{ijt}} + v_{\text{ijt}} - u_{\text{ijt}}$

$u_{\text{ijt}}\sim N^{+}\left\lbrack 0,exp\left( w_{\text{ijt}}\alpha \right) \right\rbrack$, $v_{\text{ijt}}\sim N\left( 0,\sigma_{\text{vj}}^{2} \right)$ (1)

Here $y_{\text{ijt}}$ is the value of crop output for farmer $i$ in group $j$ at survey $t$; each $x_{\text{kijt}}$ is an input, land, planting materials, family labour, hired labour, fertilizer, or pesticide, used by farmer $i$; and $h_{\text{ijt}}$ collects production shifters, agroecological zone and crop composition. Group membership $j$ is defined by land ownership status ($j=1$ for landowners, $j=0$ for non-landowners), so ownership never appears in Equation (1) as its own regressor; instead it determines which farmers are grouped together to estimate which frontier, which is exactly what makes it possible to recover the technology difference and the efficiency difference attributable to ownership as two separate quantities rather than one blended figure. The terms $u_{\text{ijt}}$ and $v_{\text{ijt}}$ stand for inefficiency and idiosyncratic noise, respectively.

We take the inefficiency term to be half-normal. This is a practical choice as much as a theoretical one: more flexible alternatives, exponential, generalized exponential, Rayleigh, and two-sided Laplace among them, would not converge reliably in the subgroup estimations. We make no advance claim that the aggregate result is insensitive to this choice; Section 5 instead reports how far the estimates actually move under each alternative distribution. Following earlier GLSS-based work [@Adaku2022; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021b; @Ansah2023], the inefficiency variance $\sigma_{u_{\text{ijt}}}^{2} = \exp\left( w_{\text{ijt}}\alpha_{j} \right)$ is allowed to depend on farmer characteristics (age, gender, education), institutional variables (credit access, mechanization, extension), crop diversification, and a fixed effect for agroecological zone. The institutional variables in particular have been shown to predict  farmers' uptake of yield-enhancing practices [@Addae2026], and so plausibly shift the distribution of managerial performance rather than only its mean. The noise term is standard normal, $v_{\text{ijt}}\sim N\left( 0,\sigma_{\text{vj}}^{2} \right)$ [@Belotti2013].

A farmer's efficiency relative to their own group's frontier is then $\text{TE}_{\text{ijt}} = \ E\left\lbrack \exp\left( - u_{\text{ijt}} \right)|{\widehat{\varepsilon}}_{\text{ijt}} \right\rbrack$ (2)

The second stage pools predicted output across both tenure groups to fit a meta-frontier enveloping the two group-specific frontiers:

$f^{M}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right) = \ln{\widehat{y}}_{\text{ijt}} = \beta_{0M} + \sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{\text{kM}}\ln x_{\text{kiMt}}} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}^{}{\sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{\text{skM}}\ln x_{\text{kiMt}}\ln x_{\text{siMt}}}} + \beta_{h}h_{\text{ijt}} - u_{\text{Mijt}}$ (3)

The meta-frontier inefficiency term $u_{\text{iM}}\sim N^{+}\left( 0,\exp\left( w_{i}\alpha_{M} \right) \right) > 0$ guarantees $f^{j}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right) \leq f^{M}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right)$: no group's frontier can lie above the meta-frontier by construction. The ratio of the two therefore gives the Technology Gap Ratio (TGR):

$\text{TGR}_{\text{ijt}} = \frac{f^{j}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right)}{f^{M}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right)} = e^{- u_{\text{iM}}} \leq 1$ (4)

A TGR close to one means a group's technology is nearly as good as the best in the sample; multiplying it by TE gives Meta-Technical Efficiency (MTE), a farmer's performance measured against that sample-wide best rather than only against their own group:

$\text{MTE}_{\text{ijt}} = \ f^{j}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right)\left\lbrack f^{M}\left( x_{\text{ijt}} \right)e^{v_{\text{ijt}}} \right\rbrack^{- 1} = \text{TGR}_{\text{ijt}} \times \text{TE}_{\text{ijt}}$ (5)

Every parameter is estimated by maximum likelihood. Input elasticities come from the first partial derivatives of the fitted frontier evaluated at mean input levels, and returns to scale from summing those elasticities.

## Identification Strategy and Matched Sample Construction

Landowners and non-landowners are not randomly assigned to tenure status, making a direct comparison potentially confounded by differences in farmer, household, and production characteristics. We therefore use matching to construct a balanced sample of landowners and non-landowners with similar observable characteristics. Each landowner is matched one-to-one with the most similar non-landowner based on observed farmer, household, and production characteristics. To ensure that matches are drawn from comparable institutional and geographic settings, matching is restricted to farmers within the same gender, GLSS wave, region, agroecological zone, and rural or urban setting. The resulting differences in TGR, TE, and MTE should therefore be interpreted as conditional associations within the matched sample rather than causal effects of land ownership.

The covariates used for matching capture farmer demographics, household characteristics, and production structure. They include age, education, marital status, religion, ethnicity, and relationship to the household head; household size, dependency ratio, and female share; crop diversification; and the shares of cultivated land allocated to different crops. These variables are intended to balance observable differences that may be associated with both tenure status and farm performance. Matching, however, cannot account for unobserved factors such as inherited land quality, soil characteristics, household wealth, proximity to markets and roads, or farmers’ positions within customary institutions. Addressing such sources of selection would require an exogenous source of variation in land ownership, such as an instrument that predicts tenure status without directly affecting farm performance, which is not available in the GLSS.

The interpretation of the matching exercise (`r xref("parity_unmatched")`) also depends on how tenure status is measured. Farmers are classified as landowners or non-landowners using the cultivated-area rule described in Section 2, based on their reported tenure status across plots. Such self-reported measures may not fully capture effective ownership because formal and customary conceptions of land ownership do not necessarily coincide in Ghana. Much agricultural land is governed by customary arrangements that may provide secure, heritable, or transferable use rights without formal documentation, making the reported ownership status sensitive to how respondents interpret the survey question. This is particularly relevant across GLSS rounds, where the wording and probing procedures differ; for example, GLSS3 instructed interviewers to probe specifically for a title deed. Previous evidence suggests that self-reported tenure measures can contain information not captured by administrative records, but may also be subject to reporting error [@Behr2015; @Amsler2017]. We therefore interpret the matching estimates as comparisons of farmers with similar observable characteristics rather than as corrections for measurement error.

Because the matching variables combine continuous and categorical characteristics, we evaluate several measures of closeness rather than imposing a single distance metric. One-to-one matching is conducted using Euclidean distance, scaled Euclidean distance, propensity scores estimated with Logit, Probit, complementary log-log, and Cauchit links, Mahalanobis distance [@Rubin1980], and robust Mahalanobis distance [@Rosenbaum2020]. Balance is assessed using standardized mean differences, variance ratios, and Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, with values close to zero for standardized differences and Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics and values close to one for variance ratios indicating better balance [@Rubin2001; @Stuart2010]. The alternative procedures produce similar standardized differences but differ in variance balance. Robust Mahalanobis matching provides the closest variance ratios to one while remaining among the strongest methods on the other balance measures and is therefore used for the main analysis. `r xref("covariate_balance")` presents the balance achieved by each matching procedure across all covariates, allowing the choice to be assessed directly.

The results are not sensitive to this particular matching choice. The robustness analysis in Section 5 repeats the estimation using alternative distance measures and propensity-score specifications (`r xref("robustness")`). None changes the aggregate TGR, TE, or MTE estimates by more than approximately one percentage point relative to the main specification. Because the estimated ownership differences are themselves small, however, changes of this magnitude can cause individual estimates to cross zero. We therefore interpret the aggregate comparison as evidence of near-parity between landowners and non-landowners rather than relying on the direction of a small residual difference.

The five GLSS rounds are also treated separately in the estimation rather than pooled into a single cross-section. Differences in sampling frames, questionnaire wording, and fieldwork implementation make a pooled specification potentially misleading and could impose a common production technology and inefficiency structure over periods in which both may have changed. We therefore estimate the MSF model separately within each survey wave, allowing the production frontier and inefficiency structure to vary over time. TE, TGR, and MTE are then averaged across waves to summarise the ownership gap over the study period. This approach also ensures that each comparison between landowners and non-landowners is made within the same survey-specific institutional and measurement environment.

The matching design balances farmers on observed characteristics but does not eliminate potential selection on unobserved factors, such as land quality or other characteristics that may jointly influence tenure and productivity. The ownership indicator also represents the dominant tenure arrangement based on cultivated-area shares and therefore does not capture differences in the duration, intensity, or security of individual land claims. These considerations mean that the resulting TGR, TE, and MTE differences are interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects of land ownership. The household sampling weight (WeightHH) is incorporated into the frontier estimation, matching procedure, and jackknife inference to account for the two-stage stratified sampling design. The TE, TGR, and MTE estimates therefore retain the population-representative structure of the underlying GLSS samples. `r xref(c("summary_stats", "ownership_details"))` are reported without weights because they describe the composition of the analytical sample rather than estimate population means. Standard errors are obtained using a jackknife procedure that resamples enumeration areas. For each survey wave, 100 resamples are constructed by omitting one enumeration area at a time, and the complete estimation procedure including frontier estimation, matching, and meta-frontier estimation, is repeated for each resample. The dispersion of the resulting estimates provides the reported standard errors while preserving the primary sampling-unit structure of the survey.
